note: Hand-curated (2026-08-13). amt = $ thousands per year. Priorities spend from the budget; revenue policies add to it. Sources per item; keep amounts defensible and cite where each number comes from.

priorities.name: Universal free school meals
priorities.who: Free breakfast and lunch for every public-school student — the state picks up all meal co-payments at expected participation. Act 139 (2025) already covers families under 300% of the poverty line; this finishes the job.
priorities.src: Hawaiʻi Appleseed UFSM analysis / DOE School Food Services Branch FY2025 ($32.6M at projected participation)

priorities.name: Create a state child tax credit
priorities.who: A $650 refundable credit per keiki aged 0–18. Twelve states already have one; the 2021 federal expansion cut child poverty nearly in half while it lasted.
priorities.src: Hawaiʻi Appleseed proposal ($650/child); cost modeled as $650 × ~284,000 keiki (ACS under-18), before any income cap

priorities.name: Expand the renewable energy tax credit
priorities.who: The rooftop-solar credit (HRS 235-12.5) is only partly refundable, so the households with the highest power bills get the least of it and renters get none. This adds battery storage and makes it fully refundable below the state median income.
priorities.src: DOTAX Tax Credits Claimed by Hawaii Taxpayers (RETITC runs ~$60-90M/yr recently); MODELED expansion, not the existing credit's cost

revenue.name: Tax the wealth of multi-millionaires
revenue.who: An annual 2-percent tax on net worth above $20 million.
revenue.src: Modeled, not a fiscal note. Estimate pending.

_retiredRevenue.name: Modernize the conveyance tax
_retiredRevenue.who: Rates haven't moved since 2009. Marginal rates cut the tax for most residents while raising it on high-value investment property and out-of-state buyers (HB 2049-style).
_retiredRevenue.src: Hawaiʻi Budget Primer FY2026-27 tax-fairness section: $70–80M/yr (midpoint used)

_retiredRevenue.name: Tax investment profits like paychecks
_retiredRevenue.who: Capital gains are taxed at 7.25% while wages pay up to 13%. Taxing them as ordinary income raises $85–132M a year — 88% of it from the top 1%.
_retiredRevenue.src: Hawaiʻi Budget Primer FY2026-27 / ITEP: $85–132M/yr (midpoint used)

_retiredRevenue.name: Close corporate loopholes
_retiredRevenue.who: Worldwide combined reporting stops multinationals from shifting the profits they earn in Hawaiʻi offshore — the same standard small local businesses already meet.
